title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Staying Near Termini” sells Termini’s “Unbeatable transport”; “The Rome Metro, Made Simple” says the Pantheon, Navona and Trevi have no stops. Neither adds that the Termini discount buys a line that skips the core. Sleep in Centro Storico or Monti.

articles.title: Is Staying Near Termini a Good Idea?
articles.full_title: Is Staying Near Termini a Good Idea?
articles.fact_quoted: Unbeatable transport. Both metro lines (A and B) meet here

articles.title: The Rome Metro, Made Simple
articles.full_title: The Rome Metro, Made Simple
articles.fact_quoted: Not great for: the dense historic center (Pantheon, Navona, Trevi, Campo de' Fiori) — there are no metro stops there, so you walk

book_call_quoted: Sleep inside the core; treat a metro address as a downgrade, not a discount.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Is the Roma Pass Worth It?” asks you to estimate your transport; “Where to Stay for a First Visit” says a historic-center base means you “almost never need transit.” Neither adds that the hotel already did the pass math. Skip the pass; tap a card.

articles.title: Is the Roma Pass or Omnia Card Worth It?
articles.full_title: Is the Roma Pass or Omnia Card Worth It?
articles.fact_quoted: Estimate your transport — if you're mostly walking, it's near zero; if you're criss-crossing, it adds up.

articles.title: Where to Stay for a First Visit
articles.full_title: Where to Stay in Rome for a First Visit
articles.fact_quoted: You step out of your hotel into the Rome of postcards, and you almost never need transit.

book_call_quoted: If you slept in the core, skip the pass and tap a contactless card.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “The Leonardo Express” runs about €14 a head to Termini; “Taxis in Rome” fixes €55 for up to four inside the Walls; “Where to Stay” sends you to the historic center. None prices the train door to door to that hotel. Two with bags: taxi.

articles.title: The Leonardo Express
articles.full_title: The Leonardo Express & Train Options from Fiumicino
articles.fact_quoted: Fare: a fixed ~€14 one-way for adults (check the current price)

articles.title: Taxis in Rome
articles.full_title: Taxis in Rome: Fares, Apps & Avoiding Overcharges
articles.fact_quoted: €55 from Fiumicino (FCO) and €40 from Ciampino (CIA) to anywhere inside the Aurelian Walls (essentially all of central Rome), covering up to four passengers with luggage.

articles.title: Where to Stay for a First Visit
articles.full_title: Where to Stay in Rome for a First Visit
articles.fact_quoted: for a first visit, base yourself in or near the historic center (Centro Storico) so you can walk to most of what you came for.

book_call_quoted: Central base, first night, real luggage: take the fixed-fare taxi and don’t feel fleeced.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Public Transport Tickets” prices a day pass for “Colosseum in the morning, Vatican in the afternoon”; the “Combined Ticket” guide calls that a death march; “Where to Stay” puts Monti at ancient Rome’s door. Together: walk to the Forum at opening, Vatican another day.

articles.title: Public Transport Tickets & the Roma Pass
articles.full_title: Public Transport Tickets & the Roma Pass
articles.fact_quoted: For a full sightseeing day — Colosseum in the morning, Vatican in the afternoon, Trastevere for dinner — you'll easily clear that, so the day pass wins.

articles.title: The Combined Ticket
articles.full_title: The Colosseum, Forum & Palatine: One Ticket, Explained
articles.fact_quoted: stacking the Vatican on top of it turns a great day into a death march

articles.title: Where to Stay for a First Visit
articles.full_title: Where to Stay in Rome for a First Visit
articles.fact_quoted: The Colosseum side (Monti, the historic-center east) puts ancient Rome on your doorstep

book_call_quoted: Give the ancient core its own half-day, and start with the Forum at opening.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Vatican Museums Tickets” says pricier options add tours, “not a faster security line”; “St. Peter's Without the Wait” keeps the basilica passage for guided tours. So a premium buys off one queue, the square’s, and only with a guide. Book official; pay only for a guide you want.

articles.title: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel Tickets
articles.full_title: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel: Tickets & Timing
articles.fact_quoted: higher-priced options add guided tours or special access, not a faster security line.

articles.title: St. Peter's Basilica Without the Wait
articles.full_title: St. Peter's Basilica Without the Wait
articles.fact_quoted: Note this connection is generally available only on guided tours, not to independent museum visitors.

book_call_quoted: Pay a premium only for a guide you actually want.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Rome in 3 Days” lists three timed bookings as one chore; “Vatican Museums Tickets” says summer slots go “three to four weeks ahead”; “The Borghese” says book “the moment your dates are set.” None sorts them by which vanishes first. Lock those two once dates firm.

articles.title: Rome in 3 Days
articles.full_title: Rome in 3 Days: The Ideal First Visit
articles.fact_quoted: Book three timed entries in advance: the Colosseum (Day 1), the Vatican Museums (Day 2), and the Borghese Gallery (Day 3).

articles.title: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel Tickets
articles.full_title: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel: Tickets & Timing
articles.fact_quoted: in summer and around holidays, slots sell out three to four weeks ahead.

articles.title: The Borghese Gallery
articles.full_title: The Borghese Gallery: Why You Must Book Ahead
articles.fact_quoted: Just book it the moment your dates are set.

book_call_quoted: Book the three that sell out the moment your dates are firm; leave the rest to the trip week.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Cash, Cards & Tipping” says choose euros and carry cash “but you won't need much”; “Is Rome Safe?” puts pickpockets on Line A and the 64 bus. Neither sizes the wallet: a day or two’s cash from a bank ATM, and no more.

articles.title: Cash, Cards & Tipping
articles.full_title: Cash, Cards & Tipping in Rome for Americans
articles.fact_quoted: Cash: carry some, but you won't need much

articles.title: Is Rome Safe?
articles.full_title: Is Rome Safe? An Honest Guide for Americans
articles.fact_quoted: Line A is the single biggest hotspot, particularly during crowded boarding.

book_call_quoted: Keep a day or two’s cash for small trattorias and tips, and no more — large sums are only pickpocket bait.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “10 Trattorias” puts the traps in “the few blocks immediately around” the Colosseum, Trevi and Vatican; “Walking Rome” makes most hops between sights 5–10 minutes. Neither adds that the trap belt is that thin: the cure is a short walk, not a list.

articles.title: 10 Trattorias Locals Actually Love
articles.full_title: 10 Trattorias Locals Actually Love
articles.fact_quoted: The classic Rome tourist trap clusters in the few blocks immediately around the Colosseum, the Trevi Fountain, the Vatican entrance, and the busiest edges of Piazza Navona

articles.title: Walking Rome
articles.full_title: Walking Rome: The City Is Smaller Than You Think
articles.fact_quoted: the entire classic-sights core is a 30-minute stroll end to end, with most hops between major sights just 5–10 minutes apart.

book_call_quoted: Don’t collect restaurant names; walk ninety seconds off the sight.

title: What the free guides never connect
text: “Best Day Trips by Train” budgets Pompeii at about twelve hours door to door; “Ostia Antica” says Ostia wins on little time and Pompeii on a full free day. The book applies that to a three- or four-day first trip: the spare day is Ostia, and never a Monday.

articles.title: Best Day Trips from Rome by Train
articles.full_title: Best Day Trips from Rome by Train
articles.fact_quoted: budget roughly 12 hours door to door.

articles.title: Ostia Antica
articles.full_title: Ostia Antica: Rome's Ancient Port, Less Crowded Than Pompeii
articles.fact_quoted: If you want the thrill of a preserved ancient city with minimal time and hassle, Ostia Antica wins.

book_call_quoted: For a single spare day, take Ostia Antica; save Pompeii for a trip that can spare a whole day to it.
why_drop: N4: the live Ostia article already makes the book’s call (“If you want the thrill of a preserved ancient city with minimal time and hassle, Ostia Antica wins”; “If you have a full free day and Pompeii is a bucket-list must, go to Pompeii.”), and the train article already gives the 12-hour day. No connection is left that neither article makes. Read 2026-10-26.
text_note: accurate version, only if the owner keeps the block; “never a Monday” is the one thing it adds, and the Ostia article itself says “closed Mondays”, so it is thin
